questions.question: What are GitHub Actions reusable workflows?
questions.title: GitHub Actions Reusable Workflows Explained
questions.direct_answer: Reusable workflows are workflow files triggered by `workflow_call` that can be called from other workflows. They let you define a build or deployment pattern once and reference it across many repositories, avoiding copy-paste drift.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how to reduce duplication and enforce consistency across many pipelines.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing reusable workflows with composite actions — reusable workflows run in their own isolated runner context, while composite actions run as steps inside the caller's job.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that reusable workflows can accept inputs and secrets, that you can chain them (a workflow calling a reusable workflow that itself calls another), and that organization-level reusable workflows enforce enterprise-wide standards.

sections.title: The Copy-Paste Pipeline Problem That Grows With Every Microservice
sections.content:
An organization with twenty Java microservices starts with one well-crafted CI workflow. Within six months, that workflow has been copied into twenty repositories, each with slight variations — a different JDK version here, a missing cache step there, a deploy stage that nobody updated when the registry URL changed. When a security practice needs updating, the platform team must submit twenty pull requests and hope every team merges them promptly.

**Reusable workflows** solve this by allowing you to define a pipeline once in a central repository and call it from every service. A reusable workflow is a normal YAML file that adds `workflow_call` to its `on:` triggers, declares inputs for parameters like Java version and build tool, and declares secrets it requires. Calling workflows reference it with `uses:` at the job level, passing the inputs and secrets.

The common mistake in interviews is confusing reusable workflows with **composite actions**. Composite actions encapsulate a sequence of steps that run inside the caller's job — they share the same runner and workspace. Reusable workflows encapsulate entire jobs with their own runners, their own environments, and their own logs. The isolation boundary is fundamentally different, and choosing the wrong abstraction leads to either over-scoped permissions or unnecessary runner overhead.

sections.title: How workflow_call Turns a Pipeline Into a Callable Template
sections.content:
A reusable workflow declares its contract through `inputs` (parameters) and `secrets` (credentials). The caller satisfies this contract with `with:` and `secrets:` mappings. **Input defaults** minimize configuration for the common case while allowing overrides for services with different requirements.

```yaml
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      java-version:
        type: string
        default: '21'
    secrets:
      REGISTRY_PASSWORD:
        required: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: ${{ inputs.java-version }}
          distribution: temurin
          cache: maven
      - run: mvn -B verify
```

The caller workflow becomes minimal — often just three lines per job that specify the reusable workflow path, inputs, and secrets.

```yaml
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/java-ci.yml@v2
    with:
      java-version: '17'
    secrets:
      REGISTRY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }}
```

The `@v2` tag reference is critical. Pinning to a version tag means consuming repositories are not broken by upstream changes. When making a breaking change like renaming an input, the platform team creates a new major version tag and communicates the migration path. Using `@main` means every repository picks up YAML edits immediately — a single syntax error in the reusable workflow breaks twenty services simultaneously.

sections.title: Versioning, Secrets Forwarding, and Organization-Wide Enforcement
sections.content:
For organizations managing dozens of repositories, three capabilities make reusable workflows practical at scale. First, **`secrets: inherit`** in the caller forwards all available secrets without listing each name individually. This reduces boilerplate when the reusable workflow needs five or six secrets, though it trades convenience for the principle of least privilege.

Second, reusable workflows support **outputs** that flow back to the caller. A build workflow can expose the Docker image tag as an output that a separate deploy workflow consumes. This chains reusable workflows into multi-stage pipelines where each stage is independently maintainable.

Third, **organization rulesets** can require every repository to call the approved central CI workflow before merging. This enforcement mechanism means individual teams cannot bypass the standard pipeline — they can extend it by adding jobs before or after the reusable workflow call, but they cannot skip it. For compliance-heavy industries, this guarantees that every service passes the same security scans and quality gates.

The versioning strategy deserves explicit mention. Semantic versioning through Git tags (`@v1`, `@v2`) lets the platform team iterate on the pipeline without disrupting consumers. Release notes on GitHub releases communicate changes, and keeping the previous major version supported for at least one quarter gives teams time to migrate. This discipline turns a shared workflow from a fragile dependency into a reliable internal product.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`workflow_call` marks a workflow as callable** — platform teams publish one golden pipeline instead of maintaining twenty forked copies that drift apart across microservice repositories
- **Job-level `uses:` runs in an isolated runner** — unlike composite actions that share the caller's workspace and job context, reusable workflows get their own runner and log stream with separate environment scope
- **Declared `inputs` and `secrets` document the contract** — callers must satisfy required parameters or the workflow fails fast, preventing silent misconfiguration when a team forgets to pass a registry password
- **`@v2` tag pinning prevents upstream breakage** — version tags let the platform team iterate while consuming repositories control when they adopt changes, unlike `@main` which propagates every commit instantly
- **`secrets: inherit` reduces boilerplate forwarding** — avoids listing dozens of secret names in every microservice caller, though it trades least-privilege for convenience at the org-secret level

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Reusable workflows in GitHub Actions let one repository define a workflow that other repositories (or other workflows in the same repository) can call. They solve the copy-paste problem that emerges when 30 microservice repositories all have identical CI pipelines.

**Defining a reusable workflow**
- A reusable workflow uses `on: workflow_call:` instead of push or pull_request triggers — this marks it as callable by other workflows, not directly triggerable by events
- Define `inputs:` and `secrets:` blocks to parameterize the workflow — `java-version` as an input, `DOCKER_PASSWORD` as a secret that the caller passes through; the reusable workflow does not have access to the caller's secrets unless explicitly passed
- Publish reusable workflows in a dedicated `.github` repository in your organization — `org/.github/.github/workflows/java-ci.yml`; callers reference it as `uses: org/.github/.github/workflows/java-ci.yml@main`

**Calling a reusable workflow**
- A caller workflow invokes a reusable workflow with `uses: org/.github/.github/workflows/java-ci.yml@v1.2` and passes inputs and secrets with `with:` and `secrets:` blocks
- `secrets: inherit` passes all of the caller's secrets to the reusable workflow without listing them individually — convenient but removes the explicit contract of which secrets the workflow needs; prefer explicit `secrets:` passing for clarity
- Pin reusable workflow references to a tag or commit SHA (`@v1.2` or `@sha`), not `@main` — calling `@main` means a change to the shared workflow immediately affects all callers without a coordinated rollout

**Governance benefits**
- The platform team owns and maintains the reusable workflow; security patches (updated Trivy scan step, new SonarQube version) apply to all 30 consumers on the next merge without touching any consumer repository
- Callers cannot skip mandatory steps — a `required-checks` step in the shared workflow that calls SonarQube quality gate cannot be removed by individual teams, enforcing organization-wide standards

questions.question: How do you set up code quality checks (SonarQube) in GitHub Actions?
questions.title: Setting Up SonarQube Code Quality Checks in GitHub Actions
questions.direct_answer: Integrate SonarQube into GitHub Actions by adding a `sonar:sonar` Maven goal (or the SonarScanner Gradle task) to your workflow, pointing it to your SonarQube server URL via environment variables, and storing the authentication token in GitHub Secrets.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand static code analysis integration and how to enforce quality gates in CI.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running Sonar analysis without first running the test phase, so code coverage data is missing from the report.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Quality Gate status polling, PR decoration that comments analysis results directly on pull requests, and using SonarCloud as a managed alternative to a self-hosted server.

sections.title: The Quality Dashboard Nobody Checks Until the Gate Blocks a Merge
sections.content:
Most Java teams install SonarQube, run analysis in CI, and then ignore the dashboard for months. Code smells accumulate, coverage drifts below the threshold, and nobody notices until a new engineer asks why the quality gate is permanently red. The problem is not the analysis — it is the **enforcement loop**. Without a mechanism that blocks a pull request when quality drops, SonarQube becomes an expensive dashboard that produces metrics nobody acts on.

Integrating SonarQube with GitHub Actions requires wiring three pieces together. First, the **analysis phase** runs after `mvn verify` so JaCoCo coverage data exists before Sonar reads it. Running analysis before tests means Sonar evaluates code smells and duplication but has zero coverage information, which either silently passes the gate or fails for the wrong reason. Second, the **quality gate check** polls the SonarQube server for the gate decision and fails the workflow if it does not pass. Third, **PR decoration** surfaces issues directly in pull request comments so developers see new bugs inline on the diff rather than navigating to a separate dashboard.

The critical architectural choice is whether to use self-hosted SonarQube or the managed **SonarCloud** service. SonarCloud removes patching, scaling, and infrastructure concerns. Self-hosted gives you control over data residency, custom plugins, and network isolation for air-gapped compliance environments.

sections.title: Sequencing the Build So Coverage Data Exists Before Sonar Reads It
sections.content:
The workflow must run `mvn verify` before `sonar:sonar` because **JaCoCo generates its XML report** during the Maven test phase. The `pom.xml` needs the JaCoCo plugin configured with `prepare-agent` and `report` goals so the coverage report exists at the expected path.

The workflow step combines both commands and authenticates using the **Sonar token stored in GitHub Secrets**.

```yaml
- name: Build, test, and analyze
  env:
    SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
    SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
  run: |
    mvn -B verify sonar:sonar \
      -Dsonar.projectKey=my-java-app \
      -Dsonar.host.url=$SONAR_HOST_URL \
      -Dsonar.token=$SONAR_TOKEN
```

The command runs `verify` first (which includes compile, test, and JaCoCo report generation), then `sonar:sonar` uploads the compiled classes and coverage XML to the SonarQube server. If you run `sonar:sonar` after `package` instead of `verify`, integration tests bound to the `verify` phase are skipped and coverage data reflects only unit tests.

For multi-module Maven projects, tune `sonar.coverage.exclusions` to skip generated sources — protobuf stubs, MapStruct mappers, and OpenAPI client code inflate the codebase and deflate coverage percentages. Quality gates should measure hand-written production logic, not punish teams for using code generation tools.

sections.title: Closing the Loop — Quality Gate Polling and PR Decoration
sections.content:
After the scanner uploads results, the SonarQube server evaluates the quality gate asynchronously. The `sonarqube-quality-gate-action` polls the server and fails the workflow if the gate does not pass, closing the loop between analysis and enforcement.

```yaml
- name: Check Quality Gate
  uses: sonarsource/sonarqube-quality-gate-action@master
  timeout-minutes: 5
  env:
    SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
    SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
```

The five-minute timeout is a safety valve. If SonarQube is down or the webhook between SonarQube and the action misconfigures, the step would hang indefinitely without it. In organizations where SonarQube downtime should not block all deployments, consider making the quality gate a non-required status check on feature branches while keeping it required on `main`.

**PR decoration** is the feature that changes developer behavior. When SonarQube comments inline on pull request diffs — highlighting new bugs, security hotspots, and coverage drops — reviewers see quality issues where they already work. This shifts feedback left into the review workflow rather than requiring a separate dashboard visit. Configure branch analysis in SonarQube project settings and ensure the GitHub App integration is enabled for the repository.

SonarCloud simplifies all of this for teams that do not want to host infrastructure. It provides native GitHub integration, automatic PR decoration, and quality gate checks without managing a server. The trade-off is that code is analyzed on SonarSource's infrastructure, which may not meet data residency requirements in regulated industries.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JaCoCo XML must exist before `sonar:sonar` runs** — `mvn verify` generates coverage reports during the test phase; running analysis before tests means the quality gate evaluates with zero coverage data
- **`SONAR_TOKEN` from GitHub Secrets authenticates uploads** — tokens stay out of `pom.xml` and workflow forks, preventing exfiltration from untrusted PR builds
- **Quality Gate polling action closes the enforcement loop** — fails CI when the server marks the gate red even if the scanner step exited zero, blocking bad code from merging
- **PR decoration surfaces issues inline on diffs** — reviewers see new code smells and coverage drops directly in the pull request instead of checking a separate SonarQube dashboard
- **SonarCloud vs self-hosted SonarQube** — managed SaaS removes server patching and scales automatically; self-hosted fits air-gapped compliance requirements and custom plugin needs

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
SonarQube analysis in GitHub Actions runs after tests complete and uses the Quality Gate API to either pass or fail the build based on code quality thresholds. The setup involves SonarCloud (hosted) or a self-hosted SonarQube instance, the Maven/Gradle SonarQube plugin, and a token stored as a GitHub secret.

**Analysis configuration**
- Add `sonar.projectKey`, `sonar.organization` (SonarCloud), and `sonar.host.url` to `sonar-project.properties` at the repository root — this avoids cluttering the `mvn` command with many `-D` properties and makes the configuration visible in the repository
- The SonarQube token goes in GitHub Secrets (`SONAR_TOKEN`); `mvn sonar:sonar -Dsonar.token=${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}` injects it for a single command without it appearing in logs
- Run `mvn verify sonar:sonar` in one command so JaCoCo executes and produces the coverage report before the sonar goal reads it — the coverage report must exist at analysis time; running sonar in a separate step after a step that did not produce the exec file reports zero coverage

**PR decoration**
- For pull requests, pass `sonar.pullrequest.key=${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}` and `sonar.pullrequest.branch=${{ github.head_ref }}`; SonarCloud annotates the PR with inline comments on changed lines that introduce issues
- PR analysis runs against only the changed code, not the full project — the Quality Gate for a PR checks new code quality, not the full project baseline; this is the intended behavior and makes the gate meaningful on incremental changes

**Quality Gate results**
- The GitHub Actions SonarQube Quality Gate action (`sonarsource/sonarqube-quality-gate-action@master`) polls SonarQube after analysis and fails the step if the gate status is not `OK`
- Without the quality gate check step, analysis runs but never blocks the workflow — teams see the results in SonarQube but nothing stops a merge; add the quality gate action and make the CI job a required status check to close that gap

questions.question: How do you implement environment-specific deployments with GitHub Actions?
questions.title: Environment-Specific Deployments with GitHub Actions
questions.direct_answer: GitHub Actions environments let you define named deployment targets (dev, staging, production) each with their own secrets, variables, and protection rules. Jobs declare `environment: name` to access those scoped values and trigger any configured approval or wait-timer rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the concept of promotion pipelines and how to gate production deployments.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a single job that checks an `if:` condition on the branch name instead of using proper GitHub environments with protection rules.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention combining environments with deployment status APIs for audit trails, using environment variables versus secrets for non-sensitive config, and environment-specific URLs for health checks.

sections.title: Why Branch Conditions Are a Poor Substitute for Proper Environments
sections.content:
The naive approach to environment-specific deployments is an `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` condition on a deploy step that switches between staging and production credentials based on the branch name. This works until someone pushes a workflow change to a feature branch that removes the condition — and suddenly a feature branch build deploys to production with no approval gate and no audit trail.

**GitHub environments** solve this structurally rather than through YAML conditionals. You create named environments in repository settings — development, staging, production — and attach protection rules to each. Protection rules can require designated reviewers, enforce a wait timer before execution, restrict which branches can trigger deployment, and scope secrets to the environment. These rules are enforced by GitHub's platform, not by YAML logic that any contributor can edit.

The **promotion pipeline pattern** chains environment-specific deploy jobs with `needs:` dependencies. Development deploys automatically on every push. Staging deploys after development succeeds, and production deploys after staging succeeds and a reviewer approves.

Each job uses the same `${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}` reference, but the value resolves to the correct environment's connection string — no conditionals, no branch checks, no duplication. The `url:` field on each environment records the deployment URL in GitHub's deployment history, creating an audit trail of what artifact reached which environment and when.

sections.title: Modeling the Promotion Chain — Dev to Staging to Production
sections.content:
The workflow chains three deploy jobs, each scoped to a different environment. The **`needs:` dependency** enforces ordering, and the `environment:` declaration activates the appropriate protection rules and secret scope. Each job references the same `${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}`, but the value resolves to that environment's connection string automatically.

```yaml
jobs:
  deploy-dev:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: development
      url: https://dev.example.com
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh dev
        env:
          DB_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

  deploy-staging:
    needs: deploy-dev
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: staging
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging
        env:
          DB_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh production
        env:
          DB_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
```

The development environment has no protection rules, so it deploys automatically. **Staging is restricted** to the `develop` branch, while production requires at least one reviewer plus a ten-minute wait timer. These rules are configured centrally in GitHub settings, versioned separately from the workflow YAML, and cannot be bypassed by editing the workflow file. This structural enforcement is what makes environments superior to `if:` conditionals that any contributor could modify.

sections.title: Scoped Secrets, Variables, and the Deployment Audit Trail
sections.content:
Environment-scoped secrets eliminate per-environment branching logic entirely. When you store `DATABASE_URL`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, and `REDIS_URL` in each environment, the deploy script is identical across all stages. The workflow YAML never contains environment names in conditionals — the environment declaration handles everything.

**Variables** (`vars` context) complement secrets for non-sensitive configuration. Use `${{ vars.APP_ENV }}` for Spring profile names, `${{ vars.JAVA_OPTS }}` for JVM tuning, and `${{ vars.REPLICAS }}` for environment-specific scaling. Variables are visible in workflow logs, making debugging easier. Secrets should be strictly for passwords, tokens, and private keys.

The `url:` field on each environment declaration creates entries in GitHub's **deployment timeline**. Auditors can trace which commit reached which environment URL and when, without parsing workflow logs. Combined with the GitHub Deployments API, external systems like ServiceNow or Jira can receive the same deployment events, integrating CI/CD status with change management workflows.

For Kubernetes deployments, map each environment to a distinct kubeconfig secret and cluster endpoint variable. The same `kubectl set image` step works across environments while RBAC policies differ per cluster. This pattern scales cleanly: adding a new environment means creating it in GitHub settings, populating its secrets, and adding one more job to the workflow chain.

sections.title: Verification Gates and Automated Rollback Between Stages
sections.content:
A promotion pipeline without verification between stages is just an ordered deployment script. Each stage should include a health check that verifies the application is serving traffic before the next stage begins.

For Spring Boot services, polling the `/actuator/health` endpoint after deployment catches startup failures, database connectivity issues, and configuration errors. If the staging health check fails, the production deploy never starts — the pipeline stops at the broken stage.

**Automated rollback** turns verification failures into actionable recovery. For Kubernetes, `kubectl rollout undo` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet. For ECS, redeploying the previous task definition restores the last known-good version. The key insight is that rollback should be a **first-class pipeline stage**, not a manual emergency procedure that requires SSH access and tribal knowledge.

Production approval gates add a human checkpoint between automated staging verification and production deployment. The reviewer sees staging health check results and can inspect the staging environment before approving. Combining reviewer approval with a mandatory wait timer (ten to fifteen minutes) gives the staging deployment time to soak under real traffic patterns, catching issues that instant health checks might miss.

The complete pattern — automated deploy, automated verify, human approve, automated promote — is what separates a promotion pipeline from a series of scripts that happen to run in order.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`environment:` replaces branch conditionals** — protection rules and scoped secrets are enforced by GitHub's platform, not by YAML logic that any contributor can edit or accidentally bypass
- **Same secret name resolves per environment** — `DATABASE_URL` returns the staging value in the staging job and the production value in the production job without any `if:` conditions in the workflow
- **Chained `needs:` encodes promotion order structurally** — production cannot start until staging health checks pass, preventing accidental deployments when an earlier stage fails silently
- **`url:` metadata feeds the deployment audit trail** — GitHub's deployment timeline shows which artifact reached which URL and when, satisfying compliance traceability without custom tooling
- **Wait timers plus reviewer gates enforce soak time** — the mandatory pause between staging deploy and production approval gives the application time to reveal issues under real traffic before promotion

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Environment-specific deployments in GitHub Actions use GitHub Environments with different protection rules, secrets, and deployment histories for staging and production — same workflow, different gates.

**Environment definition and protection**
- Create environments (staging, production) in repository Settings → Environments — each environment can require reviewer approval, restrict deployment to protected branches, and hold environment-specific secrets
- The production environment typically requires one or two reviewers; the staging environment deploys automatically on merge to main — this gives the team a fast feedback loop on staging while keeping production gated
- `environment: name: production` in the workflow job makes the job wait for approval and injects only that environment's secrets; a reviewer who approves in the GitHub UI unblocks the job

**Secret segregation**
- Each environment holds its own secrets: `staging` has `STAGING_KUBECONFIG` and `STAGING_DB_URL`; `production` has `PROD_KUBECONFIG` and `PROD_DB_URL` — jobs can only access the secrets of the environment they declare
- This scoping prevents a staging workflow from accidentally using production credentials — a mistake in the workflow that deploys to the wrong cluster fails with a missing secret rather than silently deploying to production
- Combined with OIDC-based AWS authentication (assuming environment-specific IAM roles), there is no long-lived production credential stored anywhere in GitHub

**Multi-environment pipeline pattern**
- Deploy to staging first; require the staging deployment to succeed before production becomes available — use `needs: deploy-staging` in the production job to enforce this dependency
- Add a smoke test job between staging and production: a few `curl` commands verifying the health endpoint and a key API response; if the smoke test fails, the production deployment never starts — a minimal but effective acceptance gate
- GitHub's deployment API records each deployment with the environment, actor, SHA, and timestamp — the deployment history on the repository page is a complete audit trail of who deployed what to production and when

questions.question: What is the difference between GitHub Actions and Jenkins?
questions.title: GitHub Actions vs Jenkins: Key Differences
questions.direct_answer: GitHub Actions is a cloud-native, YAML-based CI/CD service fully integrated with GitHub, requiring no infrastructure to manage. Jenkins is a self-hosted, plugin-driven automation server with maximum flexibility but significant operational overhead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can evaluate trade-offs between managed and self-hosted CI/CD tools and choose the right one for a given context.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Jenkins is simply 'old' or 'worse' — Jenkins remains the right choice for complex on-premises environments with strict data residency requirements.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that GitHub Actions supports OIDC for keyless cloud auth, that Jenkins pipelines-as-code (Jenkinsfile) are comparable to Actions workflows, and discuss cost implications of self-hosted runners versus hosted minutes.

sections.title: The Core Trade-off — Managed Convenience vs Infrastructure Control
sections.content:
Dismissing Jenkins as "legacy" is the most common interview mistake on this topic. Both GitHub Actions and Jenkins automate build, test, and deployment pipelines. The difference is not quality — it is **who operates the infrastructure and where secrets live**.

GitHub Actions is a managed service baked into GitHub. You write a YAML file, push it, and pipelines run on GitHub-hosted runners within minutes with no servers to configure, no plugins to patch, and no controller to scale. The trade-off is that your build artifacts, logs, and temporarily decrypted secrets flow through GitHub's infrastructure, which may not satisfy data residency or air-gapped network requirements.

**Jenkins** is an open-source automation server you install and operate yourself. You control the network perimeter, the plugin versions, the executor hardware, and the credential storage backend. The trade-off is significant operational overhead: JVM tuning, security patching, disk management, plugin compatibility testing, and on-call responsibility for the CI system itself. Large organizations often have a dedicated platform team just to keep Jenkins healthy.

The decision is not "which is better" but "which constraints does your organization face." A startup on GitHub gets more value from Actions in an afternoon than from a week of Jenkins setup. A regulated bank with air-gapped networks and 500 existing Jenkinsfiles gets more value from investing in their existing Jenkins estate.

sections.title: Where the Two Tools Actually Diverge
sections.content:
The comparison reveals that each tool optimizes for a different operational model — managed simplicity versus self-hosted control.

| Dimension | GitHub Actions | Jenkins |
|---|---|---|
| Hosting model | Managed SaaS by GitHub | Self-hosted on your infrastructure |
| Setup time | Minutes (YAML in repository) | Hours to days (server, plugins, webhooks) |
| Pipeline definition | YAML workflow files | Groovy Jenkinsfile or legacy UI config |
| Infrastructure cost | Included minutes + per-minute billing | Server VMs + engineering time to operate |
| GitHub integration | Native (PRs, issues, deployments) | Via webhook + GitHub plugin |
| OIDC cloud auth | Built-in, first-class | Manual setup with Vault or custom bindings |
| Plugin/action ecosystem | 20,000+ marketplace actions | 1,800+ server-side plugins |
| Data residency control | Limited to GitHub's regions | Full control over network and storage |
| Multi-repo pipelines | Reusable workflows | Shared libraries |
| Matrix builds | Native `strategy.matrix` | Possible but requires parallel stage scripting |
| Self-hosted runners | Supported as an option | Native — all runners are self-hosted |

Both platforms support pipeline-as-code stored in version control. Both can run containerized builds. Both have extensible ecosystems. The divergence is in **operational burden** and **network boundaries**.

sections.title: Matching the Tool to Your Team's Constraints
sections.content:
**Choose GitHub Actions** when your code already lives on GitHub, your team is small to medium, you want zero infrastructure to manage, and you need fast onboarding. It is the default choice for greenfield projects, open-source libraries, and organizations that prioritize developer velocity over fine-grained infrastructure control. The built-in OIDC support for AWS and GCP eliminates long-lived cloud credentials entirely, which is a significant security advantage.

**Choose Jenkins** when you have strict data residency or air-gapped network requirements, need deep integrations with on-premises systems (LDAP, internal artifact repositories, legacy ticketing), have a large existing Jenkins investment with hundreds of Jenkinsfiles, or require fine-grained access control managed by a dedicated platform team. Jenkins also has more mature support for complex pipeline orchestration across heterogeneous infrastructure — a single Jenkins controller can manage builds on Linux, Windows, and macOS agents with different toolchains.

Many large companies run both. **GitHub Actions handles standard microservice pipelines** where speed and developer experience matter. **Jenkins handles legacy workloads** and on-premises builds where network access to internal systems is required. Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners bridge the gap, giving you the YAML workflow experience with runners inside your network perimeter. The winning interview answer acknowledges both ecosystems and explains when each one earns its complexity.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hosted minutes vs owned Jenkins fleet** — Actions bills per-minute for GitHub-hosted runners; Jenkins shifts cost to VMs, security patching, and the engineering time of a platform team maintaining controllers
- **YAML workflows vs Groovy Jenkinsfiles** — both are pipeline-as-code, but Actions stays declarative while Jenkins Pipeline can express arbitrary logic at the cost of Groovy fluency and shared library discipline
- **Native GitHub OIDC eliminates stored credentials** — short-lived federation to AWS/GCP is first-class in Actions; Jenkins typically requires Vault or custom credential bindings for the same capability
- **Marketplace actions vs Jenkins plugins** — Actions composes small reusable steps per job; Jenkins plugins often imply controller-global configuration state that affects all jobs on the instance
- **Data residency determines the decision** — Jenkins wins when workloads cannot leave your network perimeter; Actions needs GitHub Enterprise Server or self-hosted runners for equivalent control

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GitHub Actions and Jenkins are both CI/CD platforms — GitHub Actions is a managed cloud service deeply integrated with GitHub, Jenkins is a self-hosted open-source automation server with decades of plugin ecosystem. The right choice depends on where your code lives and how much you want to manage.

**GitHub Actions — managed simplicity**
- Zero infrastructure to manage: GitHub provides managed runners (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) with automatic scaling; no Jenkins master/agent setup, no capacity planning, no agent OS patching
- YAML-based workflows live in the repository alongside code — visibility, version control, and review happen naturally; new contributors see exactly how the project is built and deployed on day one
- GitHub OIDC integration enables keyless authentication to AWS, GCP, and Azure — no long-lived credentials stored anywhere; the IAM role is assumed using a JWT signed by GitHub's OIDC provider; this is a significant security advantage over Jenkins credential management

**Jenkins — customization and control**
- Jenkins has 1,800+ plugins covering every integration imaginable — JIRA ticket creation, Artifactory promotion, SAP system connections; if a workflow exists somewhere in the world, there is probably a Jenkins plugin for it
- On-premise runners keep code and build artifacts entirely within the corporate network — required in regulated industries (banking, healthcare, defense) where code cannot leave the network even to run on a managed cloud runner
- Shared libraries (Groovy) in Jenkins enable complex reuse with full programming language expressiveness; GitHub Actions reusable workflows are more constrained

**Decision guidance**
- Greenfield project on GitHub with a team that wants low operational overhead → GitHub Actions is the clear choice; start there and only reconsider if you hit a specific limitation
- Enterprise with existing Jenkins investment, many integrations, on-premise requirements, or a dedicated platform engineering team → Jenkins remains the better choice
- Hybrid is common: GitHub Actions for open-source and new projects, Jenkins for legacy enterprise workflows; the platforms can coexist and even trigger each other via webhooks

questions.question: How do you trigger workflows on pull requests and protect branches?
questions.title: Triggering Workflows on Pull Requests and Protecting Branches
questions.direct_answer: Use `on: pull_request:` to trigger a workflow when PRs are opened or updated, then enable branch protection rules in GitHub settings to require that workflow's status check to pass before merging.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how CI integrates with GitHub's code review workflow to prevent broken code from reaching protected branches.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Triggering workflows only on `push` to main, which means broken code is merged before CI catches it, rather than blocking the merge via PR checks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `pull_request_target` for workflows that need write access while running against fork PRs, concurrency groups to cancel redundant runs, and `paths:` filters to run only relevant checks when specific files change.

sections.title: Catching Broken Code Before It Reaches Main, Not After
sections.content:
The most common CI pipeline mistake is triggering workflows only on `push` to main. By the time CI runs, the broken code is already merged — the team discovers the failure after the fact, and the fix requires another commit, another review, and another merge. **Pull request triggers** flip this model by running CI before the merge happens, blocking the PR until checks pass.

The `pull_request` event fires on three actions by default: when a PR is opened, when new commits are pushed to the PR branch (synchronize), and when a reopened PR resumes. GitHub runs the workflow against a **temporary merge commit** — the hypothetical result of merging the PR branch into the base. This means CI tests the code as it would exist after merging, catching integration conflicts that would not appear from testing the branch in isolation.

Branch protection rules complete the loop. In repository settings, you configure the main branch to require specific status checks to pass before the merge button is enabled. Without this configuration, the workflow runs but nothing prevents a developer from clicking merge while checks are still running — or even after they fail. The combination of PR triggers plus required status checks is the foundation of a quality gate that prevents broken code from reaching protected branches.

sections.title: PR Triggers, Path Filters, and Concurrency Groups That Save CI Minutes
sections.content:
A well-configured PR workflow runs only when relevant, cancels stale runs, and limits scope to affected code. Three features make this practical.

**Path filters** restrict the workflow to run only when specific files change. In a repository with backend Java code and frontend assets, a change to `README.md` should not trigger a 20-minute integration test suite.

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - 'src/**/*.java'
      - '**/pom.xml'

concurrency:
  group: pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '17'
          distribution: temurin
          cache: maven
      - run: mvn -B verify
```

**Concurrency groups** keyed by PR number prevent redundant builds. When a developer pushes three commits in quick succession, `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the first two workflow runs and only runs the latest. Without this, three parallel builds consume runner capacity testing commits that are already superseded.

The **`pull_request_target`** event is the dangerous variant. It runs with the base repository's credentials and secrets, which means it has write access. Use it only for trusted automation like labeling or commenting — never for building untrusted fork code. Running `checkout` against the PR head ref in a `pull_request_target` workflow gives external contributors access to your repository secrets.

sections.title: Branch Protection Rules That Wire CI Into the Merge Gate
sections.content:
Branch protection rules are configured in Settings > Branches > Branch protection rules. For the main branch, enable **"Require status checks to pass before merging"** and select your workflow job name from the list. The job name must match exactly — if your workflow calls the job `build-and-test`, that is the name that appears in the status check dropdown.

A subtle trap with path filters and required status checks: if a PR only changes files outside the `paths` filter, the workflow never triggers and the status check never reports. The PR is blocked indefinitely waiting for a check that will never run. **Solve this with a skip-detection job** that always runs and reports success for unchanged modules, or use `dorny/paths-filter` to conditionally skip job steps while still reporting the check status.

For monorepos with multiple services, required status checks can target specific job names per module. The `changes` detection job outputs which modules were affected, and downstream jobs run conditionally. Each module's CI job has a distinct name that branch protection recognizes independently.

Beyond required checks, branch protection can enforce **linear history** (require rebase instead of merge commits), **require signed commits** for auditability, and **dismiss stale reviews** when new commits are pushed. The `merge_group` event adds merge queue support — when high churn causes frequent integration breaks, the merge queue serializes merges and reruns checks on each sequential integration before landing commits. This prevents the scenario where two PRs pass individually but break when combined.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`on: pull_request` tests the merge commit** — CI exercises the hypothetical result of merging the PR into base, catching integration conflicts that branch-only testing would miss
- **Required status checks block the merge button** — branch protection rules wire named workflow jobs into the code review contract so broken PRs cannot be merged, even accidentally
- **`concurrency` groups with `cancel-in-progress`** — keyed by PR number, stops stale workflow runs when contributors push rapidly so reviewers never wait on outdated checks
- **`paths:` filters prevent wasted CI minutes** — a README change should not trigger a 20-minute Java build, but a skip-detection job must still report success or the required check blocks the PR indefinitely
- **`pull_request_target` is dangerous for untrusted code** — it runs with base repository credentials; using `checkout` against a fork PR's head ref in this context exposes repository secrets to external contributors

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Branch protection rules and workflow triggers together enforce the quality bar that code must meet before merging. The branch protection rules define the required status checks; the workflow triggers define when those checks run.

**PR workflow triggers**
- `on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]` is the standard trigger for CI validation — it runs on new PRs, every push to an existing PR, and reopened closed PRs; this covers the complete PR lifecycle
- `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` checks whether the PR is from the same repository or a fork — useful for conditionally enabling steps that need secrets, since fork PRs cannot access repository secrets
- Add `paths:` filters to skip expensive jobs when only documentation changes: `paths-ignore: ['**.md', 'docs/**']` avoids running a 5-minute test suite when only a README changed

**Branch protection configuration**
- Required status checks enforce that specific workflow jobs must pass before merge; add the CI job name exactly as it appears in the workflow YAML to the required checks list in branch protection settings
- Enable "Require branches to be up to date before merging" — this forces PRs to rebase on main before the final required check runs, preventing a PR that passes tests against an old main from merging after a breaking change landed on main
- "Require linear history" disables direct merge commits and requires squash or rebase merges — enforces the team's chosen branching strategy at the repository level rather than through convention

**CODEOWNERS and approval requirements**
- A `.github/CODEOWNERS` file assigns automatic review requirements by file path — changes to `src/main/java/security/` require the security team's approval; changes to `helm/` require the platform team's approval regardless of who opens the PR
- Combine CODEOWNERS with "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed" — approvals do not carry forward when the PR adds commits after review, preventing approvals that predate the actual changes being reviewed
